# 🇬🇧 Part 1 · London in Markdown {#part-1}

[⏱️ 0:20]{.clock}

```{=html}
<style>
/* Part 1 source panels keep code compact; theme.scss wraps long lines. */
```

```{python}
#| label: ldn-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ldn_att = pd.read_csv("examples/london/data/attractions.csv")
ldn_top = ldn_att.loc[ldn_att["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
ldn_top_name = ldn_top["attraction"]
ldn_top_short = ldn_top_name.split(" (")[0]
ldn_top_visits = f"{ldn_top['visits_2025']:,}"
ldn_total = f"{ldn_att['visits_2025'].sum():,}"
ldn_n = len(ldn_att)
ldn_n_free = int(ldn_att["admission"].str.startswith("Free").sum())
ldn_entry = "Free to enter" if ldn_top["admission"].startswith("Free") else "Tickets needed"
```

::: {.notes}
Part 1 audience: newcomers to Quarto. Objective: one Markdown guide becomes HTML, Word,
PDF, PowerPoint, a dashboard and a published website. Completion: the published dashboard
URL opens on a phone. Every step has a checkpoint in `quarto-workshop/checkpoints/`; the
finished project is `quarto-workshop/examples/london/`.
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.done}
the photo shows with its credit and the link opens TfL.
:::

::: {.notes}
`[text](url)` is a link; `![caption](file)` an image. The `{...}` after the image is a
Pandoc/Quarto extension: `width` sizes it and `fig-alt` is the alt text screen readers
announce (without it the HTML image has no alt). `>` starts a blockquote. The file has
the full alt text: "Big Ben's clock tower and the Palace of Westminster against a blue sky
with white clouds." The assistant copies the photo folder; by hand it is
`cp -R ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/images .`.
Photo: "Big Ben in the sun", John Dillenbeck, CC0 1.0, file page
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Big_Ben_in_the_sun.jpg (licence and absence of
people checked 2026-10-30). The tip: 8 of London's 10 most visited ALVA attractions have free
general admission (`examples/london/data/attractions.csv`); the British Museum and Natural
History Museum visit pages recommend a free pre-booked ticket to avoid queues (checked
2026-10-30).
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.done}
`london.html` shows the title, author and date.
:::

::: {.notes}
YAML front matter sits between two `---` lines at the very top: `title`, `author` and
`date` make the title block; `format` picks the output. `.qmd` = Markdown + YAML + code.
`date: today` is filled in at render time. Delete `london.md` once `london.qmd` exists:
both would write `london.html`. Two-space indentation matters in YAML.
:::

::: {.notes}
Same source, any format. `typst` makes the PDF with the Typst engine bundled in Quarto (no
LaTeX). In PowerPoint each `##` heading becomes a slide. `format-links` lists the other
formats on the HTML page; an entry that is an object needs both `format` and `text`.
Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html and
https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-multi-format.html (checked 2026-10-30).
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 2 min

::: {.done}
the sentence shows numbers computed from the CSV.
:::

::: {.notes}
A fence with `{python}` runs when you render, and its output lands in the document. Inline
code `` `{{python}} name` `` (Quarto 1.4 and later) puts a value in a sentence, so the text
never goes stale. Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/computations/inline-code.html (checked
2026-10-30). The data folder can also be copied by hand:
`cp -R ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/data .`. The numbers on the light card are
computed by this deck from `examples/london/data/attractions.csv`: ALVA "Visits made in
2025", London rows, top ten (https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423, retrieved
2026-10-30). Only ALVA members are counted, so this is not every London sight.
:::

## 🏷️ Cell options {#cell-options}

::: {.prompt}
```text
Add a matplotlib cell: a horizontal bar chart of visits_2025 by attraction. Hide its code, label it fig-top10, add a caption and alt text. Render it.
```
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.ldn-src}
````{.markdown}
```{{python}}
#| label: fig-top10
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Visits in 2025 (ALVA)."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of visits by attraction."
attractions.sort_values("visits_2025").plot.barh(
    x="attraction", y="visits_2025", legend=False)
```
````
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-ldn-top10
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Visits in 2025 (ALVA)."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of 2025 visits to ten London attractions, longest bar at the top: the Natural History Museum is highest and Royal Museums Greenwich lowest."
ldn_short = ldn_att.assign(attraction=ldn_att["attraction"].str.replace(" (South Kensington)", ""))
ldn_ax = ldn_short.sort_values("visits_2025").plot.barh(
    x="attraction", y="visits_2025", legend=False, color="#1f6f8b", fontsize=11,
    figsize=(6, 3.1))
ldn_ax.set_xlabel("Visits in 2025", fontsize=11)
ldn_ax.set_ylabel("")
ldn_ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, pos: f"{x / 1e6:.0f}M")
ldn_ax.figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

are computed by this deck from the same CSV, so the email and the guide always agree.
Google Docs or LibreOffice open the .docx too.

# 🌍 Publish to GitHub Pages {#publish-london}

[⏱️ 0:50]{.clock}

## 🌐 GitHub Pages {#gh-pages}

![](assets/gh-pages-flow.svg){fig-alt="Three steps: your source lives in a GitHub repository; quarto publish gh-pages renders the site and pushes the HTML to a gh-pages branch; GitHub serves that branch at user.github.io/repo." width="92%"}

::: {.bigline}
🆓 free static hosting, straight from a GitHub repo
:::

::: {.notes}
GitHub Pages serves static files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PDFs) from a repository branch.
Quarto renders locally and pushes only the rendered site to a `gh-pages` branch.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
A `_quarto.yml` makes the folder a project: `quarto render` builds every listed page into
`_site/`, with shared navigation, and the dashboard becomes a page of the site. The full
file is `quarto-workshop/examples/london/_quarto.yml`: its `render` list keeps README and
attribution notes from becoming pages, and the Downloads menu links `london.docx`,
`london.pdf`, `london.pptx`, `london-email.docx`, `london-flyer.pdf` and
`london-social.pdf`. Catch-up: `cp -R quarto-workshop/examples/london/. london-guide/`.
:::

## 🚀 Publish {#london-publish}

::: {.prompt}
```text
Initialise a git repository in this folder and commit everything except _site/ and .quarto/.
```
:::

::: {.you}
```bash
gh repo create london-guide --public --source=. --push
quarto publish gh-pages
```
then on GitHub: ⚙️ Settings → Pages shows the live URL
:::

::: {.source .ldn-behind}
😰 Behind? copy `examples/london/`
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 5 min

::: {.done}
`https://<you>.github.io/london-guide/london-dashboard.html` opens on your phone 📱
:::

::: {.notes}
`gh repo create --source=. --push` creates the GitHub repository from this folder and
pushes the commits (https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create). `quarto publish gh-pages`
renders locally, creates the `gh-pages` branch on its first run, pushes the site and opens
it; for a project site GitHub configures Pages from that branch automatically, and
Settings → Pages shows the URL and status (https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html,
checked 2026-10-30). Alternative: a GitHub Action renders on every push using
`quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2` and `quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2` with
`target: gh-pages`; run `quarto publish gh-pages` once locally first, and the Action needs
Python and the packages (or `freeze: auto` with `_freeze/` committed). The finished project
is `quarto-workshop/examples/london/`; there is no checkpoint 05.
:::
